claims.claim: The retardance in subplate is higher than cortical plates at both GW24 and GW20 time points.
claims.source: The retardance in subplate is higher than cortical plates at both time points, which is consistent with the reduced myelin density in the cortical plate relative to the white matter.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: QLIPP has the sensitivity to detect axon orientation in the developing cortical plate, despite the lower retardance in developing brain compared to adult brain due to low myelination in early brain development.
claims.source: Importantly, with our calibration and background correction procedures (Materials and methods), our imaging approach has the sensitivity to detect axon orientation in the developing cortical plate, despite the lower retardance in developing brain compared to adult brain due to the low myelination in early brain development (Miller et al., 2012; Snaidero and Simons, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work on brain development.

claims.claim: Different cortical layers are visible in the retardance and orientation images at both GW24 and GW20 time points.
claims.source: Different cortical layers are visible in the retardance and orientation images at both time points.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Different anatomical structures in the developing human brain can be identified without additional stains by referencing to the developing human brain atlas.
claims.source: With this approach, we could identify different anatomical structures in the developing human brain without additional stains by referencing to the developing human brain atlas (Bayer and Altman, 2003, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the brain atlas.

claims.claim: Individual axon tracts are visible in phase image while with lower contrast as the phase image measures the density variation but not the axon orientation.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a claim of novelty.

claims.claim: The ability to resolve axon orientation in the cortical plate of the developing brain demonstrates the sensitivity and resolution of QLIPP.
claims.source: The ability to resolve axon orientation in the cortical plate of the developing brain, which exhibits very low retardance, demonstrates the sensitivity and resolution of our approach.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the method's capabilities.

claims.claim: The human brain undergoes rapid myelination during late development as measured with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
claims.source: The human brain undergoes rapid myelination during late development as measured with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Heath et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on brain development.

claims.claim: Interpretation of myelination from MRI contrast requires establishing its correlation with histological measurements of myelin levels.
claims.source: Interpretation of the myelination from MRI contrast requires establishing its correlation with histological measurements of myelin levels (Khodanovich et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on MRI validation.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological contribution.

claims.claim: A properly trained model can rescue inconsistencies in fluorescent labeling of myelin.

claims.claim: FluoroMyelin is a lipophilic dye that can stain myelin without permeabilization.

claims.claim: Detergents used in most permeabilization protocols remove myelin from the tissue and affect label-free measurements.
claims.source: We found the detergents used in most permeabilization protocols remove myelin from the tissue and affect our label-free measurements.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an experimental observation.

claims.claim: To avoid overfitting and build a model that generalizes to different developmental ages and different types of sections of the brain, imaging datasets from GW20 and GW24 with two different brain sections for each age were pooled.
claims.source: To avoid overfitting and build a model that generalizes to different developmental ages and different types of sections of the brain, we pooled imaging datasets from GW20 and GW24 with two different brain sections for each age.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a training strategy.

claims.claim: The prediction accuracy improves as more label-free contrasts are included in training for human brain tissue.
claims.source: Similar to the observations in the mouse kidney tissue, the prediction accuracy improves as more label-free contrasts are included in training but with higher accuracy gain compared to the mouse kidney tissue.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claims.claim: The additional information provided by adding more label-free channels is more informative for the model to predict the more complex and variable human brain structures.
claims.source: This is most likely because the additional information provided by adding more label-free channels is more informative for the model to predict the more complex and variable of human brain structures.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observation.

claims.claim: 2.5D model with all four input channels shows similar performance as 2D model for human brain tissue dataset due to the relatively large depth of field compared to the sample thickness.
claims.source: On the other hand, 2.5D model with all four input channels shows similar performance as 2D model for this dataset due to the relatively large depth of field (∼16 μm) compared to the sample thickness (12 μm thick), so additional Z-slices only provide phase information but no extra structural information along the z dimension. (Table 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claims.claim: FluoroMyelin was predicted using label-free images of whole sections from GW24 and GW20 brains that were not used for model training or validation.
claims.source: To test the accuracy of prediction over large human brain slices that span multiple fields of view, we predicted FluoroMyelin using label-free images of whole sections from GW24 and GW20 brains that were not used for model training or validation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as the experimental design for testing.

claims.claim: Model inference was run on each field of view and then stitched together to obtain a stitched prediction with 20,000 × 20,000 pixels.
claims.source: We ran model inference on each field of view and then stitched the predicted images together to obtain a stitched prediction with 20,000 × 20,000 pixels (Figure 7A and D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7A and D.

claims.claim: The stitched predictions are the largest predicted fluorescence images of tissue sections that have been generated.
claims.source: To the best of our knowledge, these are the largest predicted fluorescence image of tissue sections that have been generated.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a claim of novelty.

claims.claim: Myelination level was predicted in sections from both GW24 and GW20 time points with a single model.

claims.claim: Model-predicted FluoroMyelin intensities correlate with the target FluoroMyelin stain significantly better than the label-free contrasts alone.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7C and Figure 7F.

claims.claim: While label-free contrasts are predictive of FluoroMyelin stain, the complex relations between them makes estimation of myelin level from label-free contrasts challenging.
claims.source: This illustrates the value of predicting fluorescence from label-free contrasts: while the label-free contrasts are predictive of FluoroMyelin stain, the complex relations between them makes estimation of myelin level from label-free contrasts challenging.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: The neural network can learn the complex transformation from label-free contrasts to FluoroMyelin stain and enables reliable estimation of myelin levels.
claims.source: The neural network can learn the complex transformation from label-free contrasts to FluoroMyelin stain and enables reliable estimation of myelin levels.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the method's capabilities.

claims.claim: Per-image normalization commonly applied to image segmentation tasks did not preserve the intensity variation across images and led to artifacts in prediction.

claims.claim: Numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization.
claims.source: The two main issues that need to be accounted for in image translation tasks are: (1) numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization (Yang et al., 2019), and (2) there are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work on normalization issues.

claims.claim: There are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
claims.source: The two main issues that need to be accounted for in image translation tasks are: (1) numbers of background pixels vary across images and can bias the normalization parameters if not excluded from normalization (Yang et al., 2019), and (2) there are batch variations in the staining and imaging process when pooling multiple datasets together for training.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a challenge in image translation.

claims.claim: Batch variation is less pronounced in quantitative label-free imaging but remains quite significant in fluorescence images of stained samples.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the data.

claims.claim: Normalizing per-dataset with the median of inter-quartile range of foreground pixel intensities gives the most accurate intensity prediction.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 4.

claims.claim: The 2D phase reconstruction captures the density variation encoded in the brightfield Z-stack that is informative for the model to predict axon tracts accurately.
claims.source: This is likely because the 2D phase reconstruction captures the density variation encoded in the brightfield Z-stack that is informative for the model to predict axon tracts accurately.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an explanation for the observation.

claims.claim: FluoroMyelin stain intensity faded unevenly over time and formed dark patches in the images, possibly due to quenching of FluoroMyelin by the antifade chemical in the mounting media.
claims.source: For example, we found FluoroMyelin stain intensity faded unevenly over time and formed dark patches in the images (indicated by cyan arrow heads in Figure 7A and D), possibly due to quenching of FluoroMyelin by the antifade chemical in the mounting media.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 7A and D.

claims.claim: Quenching of dye does not affect the physical properties measured by the label-free channels.
claims.source: However, this quenching of dye does not affect the physical properties measured by the label-free channels.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an advantage of label-free imaging.

claims.claim: The model trained on images without artifacts predicted the expected staining pattern even with the failure of experimental stain.
claims.source: Therefore, the model trained on images without artifacts predicted the expected staining pattern even with the failure of experimental stain.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a demonstration of robustness.

claims.claim: The robustness of predicted fluorescence to experimental variations is particularly valuable for precious tissue specimens such as archival prenatal human brain tissue.
claims.source: This robustness is particularly valuable for precious tissue specimens such as archival prenatal human brain tissue.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an implication of the findings.

claims.claim: QLIPP measurements achieve diffraction-limited resolution and provide adequate time resolution for live-cell imaging.

claims.claim: The modularity of the optical path and the availability of reconstruction software will facilitate adoption of QLIPP.
claims.source: We anticipate that the modularity of the optical path and the availability of reconstruction software will facilitate adoption of QLIPP.

claims.claim: Most biological processes can be visualized with the local density variation.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a justification for the method's approach.

results.result: QLIPP provides simultaneous 3D measurement of phase, retardance, and slow-axis orientation in biological specimens using a transmission polarization microscope with liquid crystal universal polarizer and phase transfer function formalism.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C25, C31-C41 collectively describe the QLIPP method and demonstrate its capability to measure density (phase), anisotropy (retardance), and orientation simultaneously. The method is supported by detailed mathematical formalism (C35, C39), experimental validation in multiple specimen types (C40-C43), and open-source software availability (C54). The reconstruction algorithms and background correction procedures are well-documented.

results.result: A multi-channel 2.5D U-Net architecture enables computationally efficient prediction of 3D fluorescence images from label-free inputs with accuracy comparable to 3D U-Net but with significantly reduced training time.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C4, C55, C63-C72 describe the development and validation of the 2.5D U-Net architecture. The performance is quantitatively demonstrated in Tables 1-4 with metrics showing comparable accuracy to 3D models (C70) but with ~3× more parameters trainable in shorter time (C71-C72). The architecture addresses computational limitations of 3D U-Net for microscopy data.

results.result: Multi-channel label-free inputs (phase, retardance, orientation) improve prediction accuracy of fluorescent structures compared to single-channel inputs, with 2.5D multi-contrast models exceeding 3D single-channel model performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77, C83-C84 are supported by quantitative comparisons in Tables 2-3 showing improved SSIM and correlation metrics when multiple label-free contrasts are combined. Figure 4 demonstrates improved continuity along Z-axis (C76). The claim that complementary physical properties enable higher accuracy learning is well-supported by systematic evaluation across different input combinations.

results.result: QLIPP reveals anatomical regions and axon tract orientation in prenatal human brain tissue sections (GW20 and GW24) that are not visible with brightfield imaging, representing the first label-free imaging of architecture in prenatal brain tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C28, C86-C97 are supported by extensive imaging data in Figures 6-7 showing distinct cortical layers, axon orientations, and anatomical structures in developing human brain. The sensitivity to detect low retardance in developing cortical plate (C92) is demonstrated with proper calibration. The claim of novelty (C96) is reasonable given the citations to prior work and the unique combination of resolution, sensitivity, and developmental stage.

results.result: Data normalization methods enable accurate prediction of myelin distribution over large brain regions across multiple developmental time points, with QLIPP data providing higher prediction accuracy than brightfield data alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C29, C100-C122 describe the development of normalization strategies and demonstrate improved prediction accuracy. Table 4 shows quantitative improvements with QLIPP inputs over brightfield. The per-dataset normalization approach (C120) is validated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The ability to predict across developmental stages (C112) and over large stitched images (C110-C111) is demonstrated, though the claim of "largest predicted fluorescence images" (C111) lacks comparative data.

results.result: Neural network models trained on QLIPP data can rescue experimental defects in fluorescent labeling, providing more robust predictions than possible with inconsistent experimental staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30, C102, C123-C126 are supported by visual evidence in Figure 7A and 7D showing artifacts in experimental FluoroMyelin staining (cyan arrowheads) that are corrected in model predictions. The physical basis for robustness—that label-free measurements are unaffected by dye quenching (C124)—is sound. However, the demonstration is limited to one type of artifact (quenching), and more extensive validation would strengthen the claim.

results.result: QLIPP visualizes diverse cellular and tissue structures including organelle dynamics in live cells and axon tracts in brain tissue based on their density and anisotropy properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49, C61-C62 describe specific biological structures visualized with QLIPP and are supported by images in Figure 2 and supplementary figures. The physical basis for contrast (density variations for phase, myelin anisotropy for retardance) is well-established with citations (C47). The observations are consistent across multiple specimen types (U2OS cells, mouse kidney, mouse and human brain).

results.result: QLIPP is simpler to implement than prior methods, requiring only one polarization modulator and fewer images, while achieving diffraction-limited resolution suitable for live-cell imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C127-C134 compare QLIPP to prior methods (OI-DIC, ptychography) with citations (C130-C131). The practical advantages (single modulator, fewer images, open-source software) are clearly stated. Live-cell imaging capability is demonstrated in Figure 2 videos (C133). However, the claim that reconstruction algorithms are "more accurate" (C26) lacks quantitative comparison to prior methods.

results.result: 2D models show discontinuity artifacts along depth, while 2.5D and 3D models predict smoother structures; phase images provide better single-channel input than brightfield due to consistent quantitative contrast.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C79-C82 are supported by visual evidence in Figure 3 and quantitative metrics in Table 1. The explanation for phase superiority over brightfield (consistent contrast vs. depth-dependent contrast, C80) is reasonable but remains speculative ("possibly because"). The observation that this advantage disappears with multi-channel inputs (C81) is interesting but the explanation (C82) is also speculative.

results.result: QLIPP reports local phase variation rather than absolute phase and measures 2D projection of anisotropy rather than 3D anisotropy, with structures aligned along the optical axis appearing isotropic.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139, C146-C149 accurately describe limitations of the method. The distinction between local and absolute phase is demonstrated in supplementary figures (C136). The 2D projection limitation is acknowledged with citation to similar systems (C146) and physical explanation (C147). The discussion of future directions for 3D anisotropy measurement (C148-C149) appropriately contextualizes these limitations.

results.result: Mouse kidney tissue was selected as test dataset because it contains both anisotropic and isotropic structures with robust labeling; 3D U-Net application to microscopy is limited by data structure requiring upsampling and high memory usage.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60, C73 provide methodological justification for dataset selection and model design choices. The rationale for choosing mouse kidney (C56-C57) is sound. The limitations of 3D U-Net for microscopy data (C59-C60, C73) are well-explained and motivate the 2.5D approach. These are primarily methodological considerations rather than novel findings.

results.result: The 2.5D architecture provides comparable accuracy to 3D U-Net at lower computational cost, formulates translation as regression rather than classification, and enables flexible application to variable Z-slice data and sparse annotation for segmentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C168 discuss advantages of the 2.5D approach with comparisons to prior work (C158-C160). The performance comparison (C158) shows improvement over Ounkomol et al. The advantages for segmentation tasks (C166-C168) are logical extensions but not experimentally demonstrated. The acknowledgment of evaluation limitations (C163-C164) is appropriate.

results.result: The data normalization and training process enables generalization across two developmental time points, though machine learning predictions remain dependent on training data quality and similarity to new inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C173 acknowledge both achievements and limitations of the machine learning approach. Generalization to two time points (C170) is demonstrated in Figure 7 and Table 4. The discussion of machine learning limitations (C171-C172) is honest and appropriate. The suggestion for confidence interval estimation (C173) is a reasonable future direction.

results.result: Background and motivation claims establishing the context for label-free imaging, its advantages over fluorescence, limitations of classical methods, and gaps in prior work on joint density/anisotropy imaging and image translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C24 provide background context with appropriate citations to prior work. These establish the motivation for developing QLIPP and the 2.5D U-Net architecture. The claims about limitations of prior methods (C17, C23, C24) appropriately motivate the current work. These are primarily literature review and context-setting rather than novel findings.

results.result: Physical principles underlying QLIPP measurements: density variations cause refractive index changes and wavefront distortion; anisotropic density results from molecular alignment; degree of polarization reports multiple scattering and model fitness.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C51-C53 describe established physical principles underlying the measurements. These are well-established concepts in optics and microscopy, appropriately cited and applied to interpret QLIPP data. The distinction between retardance (single scattering) and degree of polarization (multiple scattering) is clearly explained.

results.result: Context claims about brain development, MRI validation needs, comparison to other polarization imaging methods (PS-OCT, fluorescence polarization), and potential applications in tractography and connectivity mapping.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C103-C104, C140-C145, C150-C152 provide context about brain development, alternative imaging methods, and potential applications. These are appropriately cited to prior work and provide useful context for interpreting the QLIPP results. The discussion of future applications (C151) is speculative but reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities.
